title: Row-Level Security
summary: Restrict which rows each user can see or change with predicate functions and security policies — and compare RLS across all four engines.

items: Implement RLS with an inline TVF predicate and a SECURITY POLICY.
Distinguish FILTER predicates (reads) from BLOCK predicates (writes).
Avoid RLS bypass and side-channel pitfalls.
Compare RLS with PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Oracle approaches.

blocks.body: Multi-tenant and least-privilege designs need per-row access control enforced in the database, not the app. SQL Server's Row-Level Security does this with an inline table-valued predicate function bound to a table by a security policy — transparent to application queries.

terms.definition: An inline TVF that returns 1 for rows a user may access.
The object that binds predicate functions to a table as FILTER and/or BLOCK predicates.
Prevents writes that would violate the predicate.

blocks.heading: How RLS works
blocks.body: You write an **inline TVF** that returns a row when access is allowed, then attach it via `CREATE SECURITY POLICY`. A **FILTER predicate** silently excludes rows from SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE reads; a **BLOCK predicate** stops INSERT/UPDATE that would move a row out of a user's visibility. The predicate typically uses session context (`SESSION_CONTEXT`, `USER_NAME()`, `DATABASE_PRINCIPAL_ID()`).

blocks.heading: Predicate types
blocks.body:
- **FILTER**: applies to reads (and the read portion of writes).
- **BLOCK AFTER INSERT / AFTER UPDATE / BEFORE UPDATE / BEFORE DELETE**: prevent writing rows a user shouldn't own.
Use both together to fully sandbox a tenant.

blocks.caption: A single query passes through the RLS predicate, which appends a hidden filter based on the caller's identity.
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TB
    q["SELECT * FROM Orders"] --> pol["Security policy"]
    pol --> pred["Predicate TVF returns rows WHERE TenantId = SESSION_CONTEXT"]
    pred --> res["Caller sees only their tenant's rows"]

blocks.heading: Predicate function + policy
blocks.body:
```sql
CREATE SCHEMA sec;
GO
CREATE FUNCTION sec.fn_tenant(@TenantId int)
RETURNS TABLE WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS RETURN
  SELECT 1 AS ok
  WHERE @TenantId = CAST(SESSION_CONTEXT(N'TenantId') AS int)
     OR DATABASE_PRINCIPAL_ID() = DATABASE_PRINCIPAL_ID('dbo');
GO
CREATE SECURITY POLICY sec.TenantFilter
  ADD FILTER PREDICATE sec.fn_tenant(TenantId) ON dbo.Orders,
  ADD BLOCK PREDICATE sec.fn_tenant(TenantId) ON dbo.Orders AFTER INSERT
  WITH (STATE = ON);
```

blocks.heading: Setting the session context
blocks.body:
The app sets the tenant once per connection:
```sql
EXEC sp_set_session_context @key = N'TenantId', @value = 42, @read_only = 1;
```
Mark it read-only so downstream code can't spoof another tenant.

blocks.heading: PostgreSQL: native RLS with POLICY
blocks.body:
PostgreSQL has built-in RLS. Enable it per table and define policies with `USING` (read) and `WITH CHECK` (write) expressions — a very close analog to FILTER/BLOCK.
```sql
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::int)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::int);
```

blocks.heading: MySQL: no native RLS
blocks.body:
MySQL has **no built-in row-level security**. The common pattern is to expose data through **views that filter on a session variable or function**, and grant access only to those views:
```sql
CREATE VIEW my_orders AS
  SELECT * FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = @app_tenant_id;
```
This relies on discipline (users must not query base tables) rather than an engine-enforced boundary.

blocks.heading: Oracle: Virtual Private Database (VPD)
blocks.body:
Oracle's **VPD** (`DBMS_RLS`) is the mature equivalent. A PL/SQL policy function returns a predicate string that Oracle appends to queries automatically.
```sql
BEGIN
  DBMS_RLS.ADD_POLICY(
    object_schema => 'APP', object_name => 'ORDERS',
    policy_name => 'tenant_pol', function_schema => 'APP',
    policy_function => 'tenant_predicate',
    statement_types => 'SELECT,INSERT,UPDATE,DELETE');
END;
```

comparison.title: Row-level security
comparison.description: SQL Server, PostgreSQL, and Oracle enforce RLS in-engine; MySQL relies on views.

code.sqlserver: ADD FILTER PREDICATE sec.fn_tenant(TenantId) ON dbo.Orders;
code.postgresql: CREATE POLICY p ON orders USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::int);
code.mysql: CREATE VIEW my_orders AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = @app_tenant_id;

migration.equivalent: SQL Server FILTER/BLOCK maps almost 1:1 to PostgreSQL USING/WITH CHECK and to Oracle VPD.
migration.different: MySQL has no engine-level RLS; you must emulate with views and revoke base-table access.
migration.directMigration: Yes to PostgreSQL/Oracle with predicate rewrites; MySQL requires a view-based redesign.
migration.syntaxChanges: Rewrite the predicate function and swap SESSION_CONTEXT for current_setting/SYS_CONTEXT.
migration.limitations: MySQL's view approach is bypassable if users retain base-table privileges.
migration.whenToUse: Use native RLS wherever available; on MySQL, layer views plus strict grants.

blocks.heading: Multi-tenant SaaS on one database
blocks.body: A SaaS app stores every tenant's orders in one table. Set `TenantId` in read-only session context at login, add FILTER + BLOCK predicates, and the same application query returns only the caller's rows — with no WHERE clause in the app and no way to leak across tenants, even if the app has a bug.

items.mistake: Relying on RLS alone while users can still run arbitrary aggregates.
items.fix: Combine RLS with least-privilege grants; RLS filters rows but users may still infer data via side channels if over-privileged.
Without BLOCK, a user could INSERT/UPDATE rows into another tenant's space even though they can't read them.
RLS predicate functions must be inline TVFs with SCHEMABINDING for performance and correctness.

blocks.body: Keep the predicate sargable (indexed TenantId) so the appended filter uses an index. Mark session context read-only. Test that dbo/admin paths behave as intended, and audit policy changes.

tips: FILTER = reads, BLOCK = writes. Memorize this.
Predicate functions must be inline TVFs WITH SCHEMABINDING.
Set tenant identity via sp_set_session_context with @read_only = 1.
MySQL has no native RLS — the correct answer there is 'use views + grants'.

blocks.body: RLS enforces per-row access in the engine via an inline predicate function bound by a security policy: FILTER for reads, BLOCK for writes, identity from session context. PostgreSQL (POLICY) and Oracle (VPD) are close equivalents; MySQL emulates with views. Always pair RLS with least-privilege grants.
